utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Today representing General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The other Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber would like to welcome all in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and all the others present in the courtroom, and especially the interpreters, who are doing a tremendous job in order to facilitate the exchange of thoughts in the courtroom. First I'm going to turn to the Prosecution in order to hear what the schedule is for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And now I'm going to ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Let me first check whether you hear the interpretation of my words into your language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You have been called by the Prosecution to testify in this courtroom. In order to do that, you have to tell us your name first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomislav Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25th May, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were your born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I currently work in a law firm in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are a lawyer, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am an apprentice lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are an apprentice lawyer. In 1993, what did you do at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a degree in law, and at that time I was the Secretary for People's Defence in Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before you take the solemn declaration, can you please tell us whether you have ever testified either before this Tribunal, an international tribunal, or before any domestic court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you be more precise. Where did you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified before this Tribunal, in the Aleksovski case and in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Can you please read the solemn declaration. Read it in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you are already used to testifying before an international court, you don't need an elaborate explanation as to what is going to happen. You are an apprentice lawyer, so you probably understand the procedure. I would like to give you some guidelines. You are going to be asked questions first by the Prosecution, because you have been called by the Prosecution to testify. The Prosecution is seated on your right-hand side. Once they have completed their examination-in-chief, the Defence counsel, on your left - we have two accused and two Defence counsel; there are five lawyers present in the courtroom but only two will be asking you questions during the cross-examination - they can also ask you questions within the scope of the cross-examination. The three Judges, who are seated in front of you, can ask you questions at any moment when they deem necessary to do so. Since you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, we expect you not to give false testimony. If it turns out that you have given us false testimony, you will be liable before the law. It is either a fine or an imprisonment up to seven years. I have to remind you of these conditions attached to false testimony. First you are going to be asked questions by the parties and by the Judges. At the moment when you are asked a question which might incriminate you, you have to notify us of that, so you can ask the Chamber to allow you not to answer such a question. Take your time when answering the questions about what happened in 1993. If a question seems too complicated to you, you can always ask the person who has put it to you to rephrase it. Take your time, because what you are going to say is very important and deserves precision, deserves some time to think about the question. If you don't know the answer to a question, you can say "I don't know" or "I do not remember." Having said that, the Judges, who are in front of you, are responsible for the running of this procedure in the most proper way. I believe that I have given you enough guidelines. We are going to begin the examination-in-chief, and for that purpose I am going to give the floor to the Prosecution. I don't know whether it's going to be Mrs. Benjamin or Mr. Withopf. I suppose it's going to be Mrs. Benjamin. Mrs. Benjamin, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Examined by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, could you state for the Trial Chamber -- could you state for the Trial Chamber, please, the municipality in which your village is located.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background and that of your fellow villagers?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is the general ethnic background of the village.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: A hundred per cent Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do national service at any time with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, could you tell the Trial Chamber the period in which you did your national service, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I served in the JNA from 8th August 1984 to 1st of July, 1985, in the School for Reserve Officers in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And subsequent to that, were you a member of any other military body?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Later on I became a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you tell us your rank and what was your responsibility.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Currently I am a major. I received that rank in May 1994, after the first multiparty elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the municipal government was being established in Travnik, I was appointed the Secretary for National Defence in Travnik. That was the name of the body, and that was on the 22nd of February, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there came a time, somewhere around the beginning of the year 1993, when there may have been soldiers or individuals other than the local soldiers in the village. Could you tell us your observations with respect to that, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Some other people appeared in -- not in 1993 but before that, as early as the summer of 1992. In the course of 1993, they came in greater numbers. They walked around with weapons. There were different units. There were -- in addition to local people, there were people from other areas of a different race, who wore different clothes and behaved in a different way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to assist the Trial Chamber with the name that these people were referred to as?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what people you are referring to. Are you referring to the local population or people who came from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ones -- the foreign ones that you said appeared on the scene. Could you tell the Court how they were referred to.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: They were referred to as Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you give us some idea as to the -- the outpost or the offices of these Mujahedins, where they were found and where they operated, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: As far as their positions, I would have to know what period you are referring to. They were not static. They did not keep to one place only. These people who arrived, they arrived as members of various Arabic humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... More specific. During the period 1993 to around March 1994, could you tell us what you know of their outposts, where they operated from.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: You could see these people in the town of Travnik itself and in the neighbouring Muslim villages. In our neck of the woods, the villages are quite intermixed and close to each other. For example, Guca Gora is a transit place. They would, therefore, pass through Guca Gora, through Travnik. They used public roads to move around. When they first arrived, they were stationed in Mehurici, to be more precise, in Jezerce, which is a part of Mehurici. This is where they had some sort of a camp. They had money. There was weapons smuggling. Those who had weapons could sell those weapons to them at a good price. They also --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to react to the translation. Page 8, line 18, the witness said that they were stationed in Mehurici, in Jezerce. Later on he said that it was some sort of a camp. The witness said that rumours had it that they had some sort of a camp. Also, the witness said that the rumours had it that they had money. Since this has not been translated in that way, I would kindly ask for the correction in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your vigilance when it comes to the translation from B/C/S into English. Witness, you have responded to a question that was put to you by the Prosecution regarding the arrival of these foreigners, and the Prosecution has asked for some precisions. According to the English translation - maybe you can read English - that you have in front of you, it has been indicated that these foreigners were in Jezerce. The Defence says that you have said that according rumours to they were in that camp. According to you, were they really there and you know or it, or did you hear it from somebody else? Can you be more precise on that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't dare go there. None of us at that time could go there. None of the non-Muslims could go to the camp and verify the nature of that camp. But I know because I saw them - I saw them passing through, going to Mehurici - and I know from conversations that I had with other people, with both Croats and Muslims from the area. I was told that the camp was indeed there. It was a public secret. We all knew it in Travnik, and we also knew that they were buying weapons. We knew that if anybody had weapons to sell, that they were buying weapons, that they were buyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. So you have specified that it is on the basis of the conversation that you had with both Croats and Muslims that you found out that that camp was in that place, that is to say, Jezerce. But you yourself have never been there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have been there, but later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the reply is satisfactory. In order to do away with any ambiguity, I'm going to put another question to you, and then I'll give the floor to the Prosecution. But we do have time today. So you have said that these foreigners arrived through humanitarian organisations, and then you went on to say that they were armed. Is it compatible to arrive within the framework of a humanitarian mission and to come armed? Is your answer with regard to the humanitarian organisations means that all those who came from abroad came with their humanitarian organisations and they were armed - which is rather surprising - or else some of them came with the humanitarian organisations and others came in different ways? Could you specify your answer to the extent that you are in a position to reply. If you are in no position to reply, just tell us so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, I don't know whether all of them - and I really don't think that all of them came with the humanitarian organisations - but a certain number certainly have. On the other hand, the fact that they have arms, I didn't say that they came along armed with the same sort of arms and that they walked around Travnik. They did carry those arms. I mean, they had arms. I saw them and everybody saw them. I don't believe that whilst they were travelling from the countries that they had come from that that they actually travelled in the same guise that they looked when they actually came. Probably they got the arms -- I mean, not probably -- They got those arms once they arrived. As to how they did that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for specifying that. Mrs. Benjamin, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, from your own personal knowledge, could you give us a description of an outpost that you would have seen these Mujahedins at, at any particular outpost. Could you give us a description, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: In the town itself? We are talking about the town of Travnik at the moment. The humanitarian -- well, at least they were called like that, relief and another one from the United Arab Emirates, one from Kuwait, one from Egypt. I can't remember exactly what humanitarian organisations -- But they had a number of premises that they had in the town of Travnik itself. I do know that they were in Plava Voda. It is a large restaurant in the most beautiful part of town. And there is a huge spring of fresh water there. And they were at the tax office. It was the tax authority's premises. Previously they were in that building, which is a municipal building. They were at the cinema. And I used to see them in the building of our Dom. It was a supermarket in the centre of town, and on the top floor they could be seen. And it is in the same building as the police station of Travnik. Maybe -- they could be exactly next door, or perhaps there is one door between those two. And then they had two nursery schools in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rajic, could you describe for the Trial Chamber the physical appearance of these foreigners or Mujahedins, as you referred to them, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Look, I used to meet them -- they did not really wear uniforms so that I could say, "Okay, this is the way one of them looked and the way everybody looked." Some of them used to wear camouflage uniforms or parts of those uniforms. They might have had just the trousers or just the top and combined with something else. And if they had trousers, they had slightly shorter ones. And then some of them used to walk about in long garments. I think in some instances they were even below the knee, some sort of dress garment which resembles what you see on TV -- what you see in Afghanistan. And they had those characteristic Arab scarves that they used to wear. I mean, you come across people wearing those scarves even today. Yeah, that was it. More or less that's the way they looked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was how they dressed. But could you tell us their physical appearance, their features, what they looked like, the complexion of their skins.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, those were people you could tell were not locals, because we look differently. They had darker skin, and most of them had beards, but not very well groomed, so to say. And darker skin. They were not blacks, but they were -- well, they looked like Arabs, because they were Arabs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the presence in the streets of Travnik, were their armed with anything? Did you see them with any weapons of any sort on their persons?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Arms were carried publicly, and they had them. For the most part, they had automatic guns, Kalashnikovs, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What of the village of Orasac? Could you tell us about the presence of these people in the village of Orasac.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Do you mean Orasac?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Orasac is a smaller Croat village which the Croats left, I think before the 8th of June, because there had been conflicts in Miletici there. There was a crime committed there. And before open conflict, there were quite a few incidents. A number of people lost their lives. And people lived in fear in those areas in which they were in minority. So they tried to save their lives and they went off to other places. If you live in a bigger village, you're a bigger group, so you feel safer. So as I was saying, after the Croats were chased away, not only from Orasac but from many other Croat villages in the eastern part of the municipality of Travnik, I do know that they went on to Orasac and they built a large facility for that area. It was a four-storey house built of concrete blocks, ground floor, two floors, and the top floor. That building is still there, only it has been destroyed -- damaged. And they also lived in people's houses. I mean, the people had left Orasac but the houses were left intact. So they lived in some of the houses, not just that building that they erected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. April 1993, and to be exact, the 9th would have been Easter in Travnik. And could you indicate to the Trial Chamber the significance of this period to you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I think it was a Saturday, the 9th of April, 1993, and it was the day before Easter, Holy Saturday. And in order to mark Easter, because Croats too were living in Travnik - fortunately, they still do - and so we decorated the town. In some places, we hung out the Croat flags near the church and the hotel and in that part of town in which the Croat population was the prevalent one. And so it was probably what triggered off the incident that followed. All the flags were taken down and set alight. There was some shooting. And it seems to me that on that day -- it's not that it seems to me. That's what happened -- In the evening, there was some sort of hunt for the more eminent Croats, doctors, lawyers, prominent people which -- who meant something for Travnik. Not just the Croat community, but the town of Travnik. And about 40 people were taken away and locked up in a medieval fortress, an old fortress of Bosnian kings that used to be used by Turks after the Turkish occupation, during the Turkish Empire. And they were locked up there. Some people were kicked or slapped or insulted, verbal insults. That was overnight. That happened overnight. And they were released the next day. I know some people who were there. I don't know all of them, but I know some names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who you refer to when you say to the Trial Chamber "they arrested," "they detained these 40 people." Who do you refer to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I mean the members of the Bosniak military component. There were various formations there, the sports company, which belonged to the police force; and then in Travnik we also had members of the 7th Muslim Brigade; and then -- well, let's say the members of the regular BH armed forces, the Bosniak military component, as it was. That's who I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time, could you tell the Trial Chamber where you were living.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: During that time, I was living in Guca Gora in my own family home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber actually when the conflict began in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Guca Gora was attacked on the 8th of June, in the early hours of the morning. More specifically, at 4.30 a.m. I will never be able to forget that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to the commencement of the conflict, days before perhaps, could you tell the Trial Chamber what you did in preparation for the conflict.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: As to the conflict, about -- for a month and a half or two months the situation had been very difficult indeed. Lots of incidents. The conflict could have broken out any moment. And basically every village organised some sort of night watch. Guards around our own houses, our own backyards. We had to try to organise some sort of shelter, some sort of protection to protect our villages. But this was going on everywhere, not just Guca Gora, because all those villages were close to one another. Unfortunately, we had to protect ourselves from the others. There was no front line there. You couldn't be sure that okay, in front of you there's somebody -- there is an enemy that's going to attack you or that you are going to attack. But it was coming from all sides. So then we simply agreed that we would guard what was ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left your home?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. A couple of days before the 8th, due to the nature of this situation, since my house is set apart a bit, 2 to 3 hundred metres away from the other house, and my uncle's house -- but apart from my uncle, who is over 70 years of age, I was the only man in the house. So we moved in closer in to the village to -- where our cousins lived. Because in Guca Gora, that's where my whole family is and we're all called Rajic. And we found one slightly newer house with a good basement, and also people from some ten other houses in the neighbourhood also came to spend the night. And during the day, my mother used to go to our own house, because also we had some animals. But I myself did not go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you indicated earlier on that the conflict began at approximately 4.30 a.m. on the 8th of June, 1993. Could you unfold -- could you relate to the Trial Chamber the events as they unfolded from that moment, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: That evening -- that night I went to bed very late. In this other people's home, there were about 30 of us there. And I -- around 2.00 a.m. I went to bed to have some rest. And very soon I was woken up by explosions and shooting from light arms. I ran out into the yard of that house, and I could see that shells were falling across the monastery and they were landing between the house where we were and the monastery. There was a kind of small valley there, and most of them were landing there. But there was shooting all around the village. But Guca Gora was not the only village that was being attacked. The shooting -- I mean, the people who are familiar with the situation would know that I'm talking about a part of Cakovici, near Hum, across Radonjici, which is a Croat village, and then all the way down to Maljine, Postinje, and then across the River Bila, Podovi, Orasac, Cukle, Grahovcici, Brajkovici. And then all around you, you could hear shelling for perhaps the first half-hour. You could hear powerful explosions and gunfire could be heard all along. And then at around 8.00, 8.30 in the morning things calmed down. There was some sporadic shooting, and it was more intense in the part of -- below Guca Gora in the direction of Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, during this time, Mr. Rajic, could you tell the Court how you felt for yourself and your family.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: How could I have felt? I saw that what we feared most was actually happening. Since I was wearing a military uniform -- well, we had sent one of us to go to the centre of the village and check out the situation in the village, and he came back rather swiftly, half an hour later, and they said, "Well, there's nobody left in the village, nobody to defend Guca Gora." We were the only ones left who had arms. There were about ten of us in that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave the village then?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: No, not straight away, because we didn't know where to go. We knew from what side we were being attacked. But where we thought we could withdraw, there was shooting. There was a great deal of shooting there. So I myself actually suggested -- well, we said goodbye to our families. I said goodbye to my sister, to my mother, to my wife, who was seven months pregnant at the time. One of my cousins had had a baby one or two nights before, so this cousin of mine said goodbye to his son. And then we went to the creek just below the village, and then we said, "Well, we'll wait until night-time and then until dark and then we'll see what we can do." And early in the afternoon, at about 1.00 in the afternoon, I could see a couple of UNPROFOR vehicles, transport vehicles. We could see them clearly on the road below, and we could see that they stopped in front of the village church and the monastery, where there was a clearing. And we could see that there were locals all around. And then we simply ran up this road going to the village and we got to the monastery, the area in front of the monastery where the vehicles were. We had to relinquish our weapons straight away. To be honest, I was quite pleased to do so. We had to get out of our uniforms. And then from the houses around the area, there were some civilians, because half of them had left by 8.00 and the other half basically stayed at home, because they didn't really know what was going on. They knew that there was some shooting, but they didn't know what was happening to other people, what other people were doing, because not everybody was grouped in one area. And I mean we were in several houses in the village, sitting in the basement, but you don't know what's going on. You can hear the shooting, but you don't know who is doing what. So as I was saying, we were there. We asked the UNPROFOR people - and I must say that they got the reinforcement Warrior tanks, the light tanks, which were positioned around the monastery, and we were placed within the monastery. The priests had left together with a part of the population that had left on the 8th of June, and only two nuns had stayed behind. And then somebody from the BH army came to visit us. I do know that they were not getting out of the transport vehicles. But there was basically no communication between ourselves and them. But I know everybody in Travnik, the commanders on both sides, and there was nothing going on that day. But we were told to go into the church, actually. We were sitting in the church and not the monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you sought refuge in the church on the 8th. Could you tell us what happened on the 9th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: On the next day, on the 9th, that is, we didn't know who was where. But let's say we knew who was supposed to be where on that day. So we asked the UNPROFOR staff for permission to go around the village and see whether anyone was wounded or dead. But elderly people could go with the UNPROFOR staff, I think two of them, and the rest of us, who were younger, were not allowed to get out of the monastery. And we couldn't have done it anyway. And there were no Croats left in Guca Gora, except for the monastery. And then they brought seven people in who had lost their lives the day before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony to this Trial Chamber that on the 9th of June, 1993, that while you were at the church seven bodies were brought in?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise any of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise all of them, because I had known them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us the average age of these people.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the average age, but I know about all of them. Vlado Volic is my own age, born in 1959. We went to school together. And Niko Sluganovic was probably born in 1949 or 1950. Drago Volic was retired, so he was over 60. And Rudo Petrusic too, he was a pensioner and he was about 65 or 66. And the same goes for Drago Petrusic. And Stipo Kafadar was around -- was born in 1950, as Niko Sluganovic. But when he was a young boy, he lost one eye. The oldest of them was Ljubo, Ljubomir Petrusic. He was about 70 at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the bodies were made up of young and old individuals; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you assist in disposing of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Together with the others, we dug those seven graves, and that's where they were buried. And the burial ceremony was performed by an UNPROFOR priest. He was wearing an UNPROFOR uniform. He did not have any clothes that would mark him out as a priest, but I know that somebody said that he was indeed a priest, so he was in charge of the ceremony. And then when they were already placed in the graves, they were in blankets. And then a bullet hit the wall of the church and then many people just ran away. And the service was speeded up and we stayed back to, you know, fill the graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, aside from the dead bodies that were brought back from Guca Gora, could you tell us what you heard or know about that took place or happened in the village itself.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically with respect to the houses in the village, and -- how was the village after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Only one barn burned down on that day. There was no other damage. The houses were intact. Nothing had been taken out of them. Half of the people from my village work either in Switzerland or Germany, some in Austria. Everything remained intact. Later on the whole village was burned, but it was only later, during the conflict and after the peace agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to return to your home?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to your home during that time.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: It was not either on the 8th or on the 9th of June; however, my house was set to fire. The barn was destroyed, and only the concrete columns remained. And whatever was in the house was taken away. Some people told me that, firstly, all of my clothes and technical appliances were taken out and then the house was set on fire. This is what my Muslim neighbours told me. There were two houses, one next to each other; one was mine and the other belonged to my uncle. Both were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know of your other fellow villagers' houses?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: The houses were set on fire. From the part of the Nova Bila to which we withdrew, we could see houses burning. You could see it with your naked eye and especially through binoculars. So we knew exactly whose house was set on fire, whose house was it that was burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Rajic, would you be able to assist the Trial Chamber with who you think may have been responsible for the burning, as you say, and the looting, and the killing that took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel has the floor. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this witness testifies about the fact known to him, and it is not correct to put questions to this witness which go beyond his role as a witness. This question calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, you have noted the observation put forth by the Defence. The Defence believes that your question calls for this witness's speculation. He did see the houses burning, the houses that were situated in the village of Nova Bila, and from the place where he was he could see the houses burning. Witness, you have followed this discussion. The Prosecution has asked you a question, and the Defence observation is that your answer would call for speculation. The question was very clear. From the place where you were, how far away was Nova Bila from the place where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two kilometres. Not Nova Bila, but the place from which we could observe the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So two kilometres. What could you see from the place where you were at a two-kilometre distance? What could you see precisely from the place where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could see the houses burning. You could see even further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you could see the houses burning. From the place where you were, could you see the persons that set the houses on fire? Did you see anybody setting these houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I couldn't. I couldn't see anybody. I couldn't see the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So you don't know, because you couldn't see who was setting the houses on fire. How can you then infer that the houses were set on fire by the persons who could have been persons who did not belong to your community? You don't know who set these houses on fire. How could you make an inference that those people were not members of your community? You -- did you find that out only later? When you testify, you testify about the facts that you saw with your own two eyes, and if you didn't see anybody, you can't tell us who was it who set the houses on fire. Maybe you can say that later on there were rumours about who set the houses on fire. This is a difference. And the observation by the Defence was exactly that, that the Prosecution is calling for your speculation. So when they ask you -- when the Prosecution asks you who was it who set the houses on fire, what can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want me to give you the names of the people who set the houses on fire, I can't give you their names. But what I can tell you is this: Nobody else could have set these houses on fire but those who had expelled us from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you're saying is that those who set the houses on fire were the ones who expelled us? This is your inference. Is this your inference, or do you know it for a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the truth. I don't know what you want to call this truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, tell us who expelled you from your village.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be able to identify the unit from which these people came from?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: It was the zone of the 306th Mountain Brigade of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along with those members from the BH army, were there any other individuals who was involved in the expulsion of yourselves and your fellow villagers from their village?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody else. I didn't see any other people. But I heard that in other areas there were some others as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, what about the Mujahedins? Could you assist us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence have jumped to their feet, both Defence counsel, because needless to say they want to say to the Chamber that this was a leading question. Am I right, Madam Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Mr. President. The witness has clearly answered every question put to him so far by the Prosecution. He said that he was expelled by the BH army and that was the zone of the responsibility of the 306th Brigade, and that he did not see any other soldier in the area. The leading question, it has to be redacted and the witness has to be instructed not to answer a question like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my objection would have been the same, so I don't have to repeat it, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The intention of the Prosecution was to ask a question who would not be a leading question. I believe that the question was too fast. Maybe you should have arrived at the question in a different way. Maybe you should have asked the witness what he saw. And you can see on page 24, line 10, when the witness said that this was the zone of the 306th Mountain Brigade. But we do not know whether this was just their zone or whether these were members of the 306th Brigade. So the witness is not precise in his answer. I'm going to put a question to the witness: Sir, you are saying -- you know that we are here in a verbal procedure. We don't have any written documents. In order to arrive at the truth, what is important to us is what you say to us. Are you saying -- your answer has to be precise and it has to be correct. And when there is any sort of ambiguity, then your answer does not provide the answer to the question and is not helping us. At the one moment the Prosecutor asked: Who is it who expelled you? The translation into English was that it was -- you didn't say that they were members of the 306th Brigade. In the translation, we read this was the zone of the 306th Brigade. I'll repeat the question to you: Who was it who expelled you? When I say "who," that means did you see anybody, anybody who belonged to any military formation? So who was it who expelled you? Who were the persons who expelled you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can't answer that question. Nobody can answer that question, because -- if you're shot at, then you run to save your life. I was not paying too much attention to the insignia. I don't know who they were. I know who they could have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Why did you then say that it was in the zone of the responsibility of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I know that this was the zone of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So you're saying that you were shot at in order to be expelled. You don't know who did the shooting. However, since this was the zone of responsibility of the 306th Brigade, you concluded that it could have been him. You are a lawyer. You understand the importance of your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, you have the floor again. You may proceed. So the witness does not really know who was it who expelled them, because he was being shot at; but he has told us that since this was the zone covered by the 306th Brigade he deducted that these could have been members of the 306th Brigade. Mrs. Benjamin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, prior to the conflict and on the day of the conflict, could you tell the Trial Chamber who you saw in your village.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you see any other military personnel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We go back to the same thing. The Prosecutor asks you who you saw. You say, "I didn't see anybody. I saw some people. I saw a soldier of the 306th Brigade." You have to answer this question. The question was whom you saw. You either know or you don't know. If you don't know, you just tell us that you don't know. You can tell us you didn't see anybody. You can tell us that you saw somebody. If you did see somebody, you can please tell us whom you saw. Otherwise, the Defence will again object and say that the Prosecution is putting a leading question. So you must not be led in your testimony. Listen carefully and answer based on what you saw, not based on what you may be able to conclude or based on what some other people told you. If you heard something from other people, tell us so. Or if you are inferring, then you just tell us that you're making an inference. Mrs. Benjamin, I give you the floor again. Please be cautious. Make sure that the question is put in such a way so as to enable the witness to answer precisely, without you leading him. It is a bit of an art. However, you have the floor, Mrs. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. And I could not agree with you more. But at the same time, with the greatest respect, I do not think that the question was a leading question. It was a very straightforward question based on the evidence and the testimony that the witness has led before. And I don't think that I can put it in any other way except to ask him:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day in question, the 8th of June and prior to that, did you see anybody in the streets of -- of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, please look at the line 1 on page 27 and read it and see what it says. The answer is on page 26 in lines 24 and 25. You asked the witness as follows: On the day of the conflict, what were the sides or parties which were present? Whom did you see? His answer was: Members of the BH army. My translation into French - and I believe that it was the same in English - it was not an affirmation. It was a question. Can you please repeat the question, and we shall wait for the witness to reply and see what the reply is going to be. The reply was a question. It was in the form of a question, rather than in the form of an affirmation. And the Defence counsel objected to that. Can you please rephrase your question. Let's try again from the beginning. And we have a lot of time today. Mrs. Benjamin, you have the floor. Please rephrase your question. Repeat the question that is on the page of the transcript that I have just mentioned to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And that would be line 26. Could we get it back, please, line 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me help you. Page 26, lines 24 and 25. Read the question that you have put. Can you please read it again. You asked: "Can you tell the Chamber what you saw on the day of the conflict." On page 27, it says: "Members of the BH army." However, I heard him answer in his own language. The answer sounded like a question. It was not an affirmation. I believe that the Defence counsel understood it in the same way in their -- in the B/C/S. You took his answer as a fact, as if he had said that they were BH army members. However, it seemed to me that he replied with a question. Can you please repeat the question that you find on page 26 in lines 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, prior to the conflict and on the day of the conflict, which was 8 June 1993, could you tell the Trial Chamber who you saw on the streets on that day.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I will explain. On the 8th of June, in the afternoon, in front of the monastery an UNPROFOR vehicle arrived and Colonel Alagic came. He was in the vehicle. With him was Salko Beba, with whom I had worked in the exchange commission in Travnik. Salko wore a camouflage uniform, as well as Alagic. Salko got off the personnel carrier, whereas Alagic stayed on. I spoke personally with Alagic. Salko Beba wore an Heckler Koch, a short automatic rifle that is usually carried by special police. On the following day, on the 9th of June, sometime before we were transported by UNPROFOR from the monastery in Guca Gora, together with the priest, of Dolac, Ivo Markovic, Dzemo Merdan came. I know him personally as well, because we, together, took over the barracks in Travnik from the JNA. I believe that at the moment he is a high-ranking officer of the federation army. And that is why I know that what happened to us was done to us by the BH army and those who were subordinated to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Can I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, could you tell me -- or could you tell the Trial Chamber what rank did Dzemo Merdan hold in his unit.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what unit he belonged to. I don't think he was a member of any brigade from Travnik. I believe that at the time he discharged a duty in the 3rd Corps of the BH army. What his duties were, I don't know. I don't know what his rank was, because at the time he did not wear any of his rank insignia on the uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And with respect to the Mujahedins that you have spoken of before in your testimony, would you be able to assist this Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor insists on putting the question to which the witness has not replied anything that had to do with the events that took place on the 8th and on the 9th of June, despite several questions put by you and the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, you are again coming back to the issue of Mujahedins. Are you starting a new line of questioning or are you coming back to Mr. Salko Beba, to Mr. Merdan? Your question, does it stem from the fact that they were seen on the 8th and the 9th of June, or is this question going to be linked with something that you have already mentioned? The Defence believes that you are coming back to -- in order to force the witness to talk about the Mujahedin, although this does not stem from any of the questions that you have put to the witness before.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if my learned friend would allow me to finish the question, then she'd see where I'm coming from. Because the witness did indicate in his testimony earlier on, very much earlier on, of Mujahedins. And I wanted to tie in the question with the Mujahedins. But she wouldn't allow me to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Can you then repeat your question so that we can hear all of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to earlier responses given with respect to the Mujahedins, could you tell this Trial Chamber, if you can, who was responsible or who were the Mujahedins subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will have to object this time, because this time this is obviously a leading question and the witness is asked to provide his own opinion on something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. What can the Prosecution tell us about this objection put forth by the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question is -- It's a very clear straightforward question: Who was responsible or who were the Mujahedins subordinated to? This is by no means a leading question. And I would like to rule the Trial Chamber on this issue. This is an important issue, and the Prosecution wants to put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I agree with the second part of the objection put forth by my colleague Ibrisimovic. The witness is asked to provide his opinion. Before that, the Prosecutor has not established any basis based on which the witness could provide such an opinion. I repeat again: This is a witness that has been called to testify about facts, not to provide us with his opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, Your Honours, the witness is not asked about his opinion. The witness, as we got to know in the course of his today's testimony, he has a military background and he has a strong military background, and he's asked about his knowledge of the subordination of the Mujahedin. He is not asked about his opinion. It doesn't require any particular expertise on this issue; only the knowledge of the witness in this respect is asked for. Again, this is neither a leading question nor is it a question asking the witness for his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have one -- on one side we have the Prosecution; on the other side, we have the Defence counsel. The Prosecution has put a question to you about the Mujahedin and asked you to tell the Chamber who they were subordinated to or who their commander was. The Defence, on the other hand, believes that this question might be a leading question because you never saw any of commanders who commanded these Muslims and that there is a risk that your answer might be linked to other facts that you have provided us with, and then the Trial Chamber may come at a conclusion that Mujahedins were commanded by somebody and you don't know who they were commanded by. You are testifying to the facts that you personally saw. If a question is put to you as to who the commander of the Mujahedin was, you either saw the commander or you didn't see him. However, if you tell us that it was Mr. X or Mr. Y whom you never saw, then you are providing us with your own personal opinion or you are relating to us something that somebody told you. You were an eyewitness to certain events; however, if you were not an eyewitness to the command chain of the Mujahedin, you have to tell us that. I am going to repeat the question in the way it was put to you. You told us that there were foreigners who arrived in Travnik and in other places. You described them to us. So when we are talking about these foreigners that you saw, did you personally see any commander? Did they have a commander at all? Or were they people who just came and went? The Prosecutor has told us that you were also and you know what a commander is. The question is now a bit more precise: Among the people who had beards, who wore different clothes, who wore something on their heads, did you see a commander among them? What can you tell us about that? How can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tell you what I know and in the way I know it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is about the things that you know personally. Did you see things for yourself or did you read it somewhere in did you see it on TV? What is important for us is what you saw personally, with your own two eyes. That's why you have been called to testify, because you were an eyewitness of certain events. Maybe you saw certain things on TV. Maybe you read about them in the papers or you were told about them. What is important to us is what you saw in 1993 in April through June, what you saw personally. The persons who were Mujahedin, did they have a commander, somebody who was in charge? This is what the Prosecutor has asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question. I worked for the commission that investigated war crimes involving Croats in Travnik, and I was also the commissioner of the Commission for War Crimes. I spoke to hundreds of witnesses. I took their statements. On several occasions, I visited the camp in Orasac. It was in 1996, but the Mujahedin were still there. I spoke with one of them who introduced himself to us. Until the moment he came, nobody wanted to talk to us. We were in a mixed delegation of the BH army and the HVO. I went there as a person who was familiar with the area. He introduced himself to us as Abu Aiman. He spoke Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. But you are now talking about 1996. The question put to you refers to the year 1993. Now you are talking about 1996. As I've already told you, we don't have any written documents and we hear it for the first time. Maybe the question should have been put differently. Maybe it should have referred to things that you did subsequently, that you were a member of the Commission for War Crimes and that you -- that there were Croats and some other people as members of this commission, and that in 1996, at that moment you realised that they had had a person in charge. However, the question put to you refers to the year 1993, not to the year 1996. Do you see the difference? So the question refers to the year 1993. In that year, when people were expelled from the village, the question follows up on that event. So in 1993, at the moment when you were expelled from your village, the Prosecutor asked you about Mujahedin and asked you whether they had a commander. In 1993, not in 1996. If you didn't know it in 1993, then you just simply tell us "I don't know." Mrs. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect, if I may assist the Court. The question that was asked of the witness had to do with his response on page 8, lines 1 to 12, when he was describing for us the different venues in April of 1993 that he knew the Mujahedins used as units, as posts. And the question was posed in that light. In light of that fact, in light of the fact the Mujahedins were around, could you assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my learned colleague has misinterpreted the transcript. The witness has never mentioned the units. He never referred to any units, at least in that part of the transcript. He said that they used to come. He said where they were. But he never mentioned them being in units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf. Perhaps we could all take a look at page 8 and lines between 1 and 12. That's what we are going to do during the break. And we shall continue afterwards. So everybody will be able to ponder this question. Once again, I believe that we will be able to overcome this slight difficulty in no time at all and it is going to be very simple to overcome that problem. At any rate, we must have a break. It is five to 4.00. We've been working for more than an hour and a half. Unless, of course, you have something crucial to say in a couple of seconds so that the Judges have some food for thought during the break. Of course we would like to have a break, but we can still consider all these points. So fire away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, very briefly. The witness mentioned at the beginning of his today's testimony the arrival of Mujahedin in the area of Travnik. Later on a very simple question based on this was asked: To whom were the Mujahedin subordinated to? This is not a leading question. This is not a question asking the witness for his opinion. And the Defence objected. I would suggest -- I would strongly suggest to in such a situation to rule on the objection. Then the answer will be very clear: Either the Prosecution is allowed to ask this question or not; otherwise, we are going to waste time and time. I really request the Trial Chamber to rule whether the Prosecution is allowed to ask the witness to whom were the Mujahedin subordinated to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We shall consider it. It is five to 4.00, and we shall continue with the hearing at 25 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. We can continue with our session. The Trial Chamber has deliberated longer than planned, so we've exceeded the time for the break that I had indicated in the beginning. Now, the decision of the Trial Chamber, with regard to the objections raised by the Defence, is the following: The Trial Chamber, having deliberated the matter, has reached the conclusion that the witness in the beginning of the examination-in-chief has referred to the presence of Mujahedin in Travnik in 1992 and 1995. Apart from that, the Trial Chamber has reached the conclusion that afterwards the questions referred to the events in Guca Gora on the 8th and 9th of June, 1993. Within this context, the Prosecution has then asked the witness a question about the Mujahedin. That question, according to the transcript, and from the Trial Chamber's point of view, had no link with the events of Guca Gora. That question, put in that way, could have given the impression that it was linked to the events in Guca Gora. The Trial Chamber believes that the Prosecution may put to the witness a question about the link of subordination in relation to the Mujahedin, but only on the basis of what he had previously stated with regard to the situation in Travnik and on the basis of his own experience in Travnik; and not with regard to the results that he is supposed to have obtained himself in 1996 whilst being a member of a commission of inquiry on war crimes. All this is to say is the question about the Mujahedin, following a question about the events in Guca Gora, gives the impression is that the Prosecution wishes to establish a link, and therefore it is not possible to establish that link. All right, then. Now I'll give the floor back to the Prosecution, who may of course ask any questions of the witness relating to the subordination ring; but only with regard to 1993, when the witness saw for himself that there was this presence in the area and not in relation to some extrapolated conclusions or rumours that he might have heard or the results of a later inquiry in 1996. Apart from that, the Trial Chamber believes that it would also be useful in order for us to properly judge the situation, perhaps either the Prosecution or the Defence could ask the witness to give us some information as to his participation in the work of that commission of inquiry in 1996; why and how he participated in that work, to what purpose, what was the nature of that commission, what was their competencies, their remit, their nature. But all that of course must be kept separate from the matter of the Mujahedin in 1993. And if this is mentioned today, this is not in order to reply to questions about the results of the commission of inquiry in 1996 but only in relation to the events that he has witnessed himself in 1993. Mr. Withopf, you have the floor. However, the Trial Chamber has indeed indicated that the question just gave the impression. We did not say that it was your intention to. It is just a subjective impression on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, at the beginning of you explaining your decision on this issue, you are making reference to the fact -- to the alleged fact that the witness was testifying about the arrival of Mujahedin in 1992 in the area of Travnik and later on in 1995, and that therefore the events in Guca Gora in 1993 could not be of any -- it could not be of any context. May I please draw the Chamber's attention to the answer of the witness. The question was: "Thank you. Now, there came a time, somewhere around the beginning of the year 1993, when there have been soldiers or individuals other than the local soldiers in the village. Could you tell us your observations in respect to that, please." Answer: "Some other people appeared in -- not in 1993 but before that, as early as the summer of 1992. In the course of 1993, they came in greater numbers. They walked around with weapons." And later on the witness asked whether there was a certain name. The witness referred to these foreign people. He answered: "They were referred to as Mujahedin." That means the witness has testified that Mujahedin arrived in Travnik in 1992 and in 1993. That means the question, to whom were they subordinated, is related to an answer the witness gave to a previous question. Guca Gora, as Your Honours certainly know from the indictment, Guca Gora is a village within the municipality of Travnik. That means the witness has said in 1993 there were Mujahedin in Travnik. And the question was: "Who was the commander of the Mujahedin in Travnik?" And this was in relation to an attack which was done in a wider area of Travnik. So the Prosecution, with all due respect, is still of the opinion that this question can be asked. It's not a leading question. It doesn't require particular expertise. Therefore, the Prosecution, with all due respect, asks to reconsider the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. I'm turning to the Defence. You have heard what the Prosecution has said. They're saying that the witness has explained to us that foreigners, described as Mujahedin, arrived at Travnik in 1992 and 1993. The Prosecution is stressing that the events of Guca Gora, which happened in 1993, are characterised by the specific fact that Guca Gora is within the administrative area of the municipality of Travnik, and therefore the Prosecution is entitled to ask the question about the subordination link of the Mujahedin in Travnik. Whilst of course, including the fact that if there is a reply to be given to that question, that would also cover the fact that the events of Guca Gora which took place in June 1993 could have been committed by the Mujahedin. Okay, so this is the theory put forward by the Prosecution and they are asking us to revise our decision. Now, I'm turning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone please to the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that you should stick to your decision because following a number of questions put to the witness by the Prosecution and put by the Judges to the witness, he gave a comprehensive account of what he saw in Guca Gora in June and also in relation to the Mujahedin. Now, the direct link between what he saw and described before the Court and that, with regard to the conflict on the 8th -- 9th of June, has nothing to do with the account of the Mujahedin from earlier on. I don't know what the Prosecution's intention is, and I don't want to try and interpret it. But I believe that after -- even after the clarification put forward by my learned colleague, there's no reason why we should in conjunction with the events of the 8th and the 9th of June ask any question of this witness with regard to the command for the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no comment at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to withdraw for a couple of minutes. Don't go away. --- Break taken at 4.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue with the hearing. Having deliberated again, the Trial Chamber believes that the Prosecution probably has not quite grasped what we said in the beginning. We have indeed indicated that the Prosecution was free to put any questions to the witness relating to the presence of the Mujahedin in Travnik in 1992 and 1993, and the subordination link of those Mujahedins. So the Prosecution may ask the question. We even went on to say that the witness could also be asked questions concerning the conclusions that he himself had reached in 1996 within the framework of that commission, but at that stage he would not be acting as a direct witness but he would be relating secondhand account. So I believe that it is an error of appreciation regarding the scope of our decision. We're not going to revise our decision, which gives you the possibility to put questions to the witness about the Mujahedin and the subordination link of those Mujahedin and any people, units or military entities. So you may ask the question. You're not banned from asking the question. All right, then. So I'm turning to you. I believe that it is probably a point of understanding. Mrs. Benjamin, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think my friends would have preferred me to ask the question in chronological order, but it's just it was my style and I choose to ask it at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Rajic, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that's where -- that's the origin of the problem. If the question had been asked in the chronological order, we would not have had this situation. It's the fact that you've turned things upside down a bit which has given us this impression. So it is for this reason that the Trial Chamber has indeed said that we thought that there was no intention on your part to ask a leading question. But it is a possible impression, which one may get. But it is due to the fact that you have not asked your questions in a chronological order. So please try and follow the chronological order of events and then we'll avoid this sort of problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, could you tell the Trial Chamber whom do you think the Mujahedins were subordinated to.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who they were subordinated to, but I think that they were not subordinated to brigade commanders. On one occasion, when a joint commission was set up in order to go to Orasac - and this commission consisted of Colonel Zimic, Adnan Solakovic - I don't know what his rank was - they represented the General Staff of the BH army. On behalf of the HVO, there was Mr. -- Colonel Slavicek --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think the witness is a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about the period 1993. Originally the question was asked of you with respect to events that took place on the 9th of April, 1993. And based on your response, I am now asking you the question: Who do you think the Mujahedins were subordinated to then?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I believe that they were subordinated to the command of the 3rd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would your answer be the same for the 9th of June, 1993 as well, for clarification to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you asked me about the 9th of June, my answer would be the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Much obliged. Mr. Rajic, could you tell the Trial Chamber where you live at present.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I live in Vitez, which is adjacent to the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question for you, just for clarification. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little while ago, to the Prosecutor's question you said that you believed that on the 9th of April and on the 9th of June the Mujahedin had been subordinated to the 3rd Corps. What do you base this claim on? How did you arrive at that opinion? Why did you say that? One may be speculating. One may be putting forth opinions. What is your basis for being so sure when you say that? When you say "I believe," does that mean that you're absolutely sure that this was a fact or is this just your opinion? In addition to that, why on the 9th of April, why on the 9th of June?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: This is just the logic of a soldier's way of thinking. This area where Mujahedin were, in Travnik the Mujahedin were in the area of the 3rd Corps of the BH army. Later on I was able to confirm this opinion of mine when we went to visit Orasac in the municipality of Travnik where the Mujahedin camp was. This camp was supposed to be visited by a joint commission which consisted of the BH army and the HVO. I've already mentioned the names of people that represented the BH army and those that represented the HVO. When we asked for the permission to visit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you in Orasac? On what date?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I was not allowed to visit, but Colonel Zimic went. Adnan Solakovic went there; Colonel Ivan Slavicek, who was a representative of the HVO. They all went there. I was not allowed to go there a member of this delegation, but I did go with them together to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When was that? When?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: That was at the end of winter, the beginning of spring 1996, but I can't be sure of the year. I can't remember exactly which year it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to the Defence for their cross-examination. I would just like to say to the witness that according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, any cross-examination has various objectives: Firstly, to make sure that you are a credible witness, that what you have told is indeed the truth, that you have related the facts that are directly connected with the facts; and the Defence can also ask you questions about the military-political context of the time; and judging from the experience, first you are going to be asked general questions about the context and then more precise questions about the facts. I am turning to the Defence for their cross-examination. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Rajic. I am Edina Residovic, and I defend General Hadzihasanovic. As the President of the Trial Chamber has already told you, I'm going to be asking you questions firstly about the general context, as I believe that you have personal knowledge about a number of these questions and that you can assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to inform you, Mr. President, that these questions that relate to the general situation in Travnik and in the area are of interest for the defence of my client and I would kindly ask you, for that reason, to allow me to put such questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, I would also kindly ask you to make a break between my question and your answer, because as you know, we speak the same language and both my question and your answer are being interpreted into two languages. We would like to help the interpreters help us understand each other and help the Trial Chamber understand us as well. When you were answering my learned friend's questions and the questions of the Trial Chamber, you said that you have already appeared in two cases before this Tribunal, in the Aleksovski case and in the Blaskic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On both occasions, you were a Defence witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Aleksovski case, you testified in August 1998; and in the Blaskic case, you testified in December of the same year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these two occasions, you gave a statement to the OTP. This was in February 2000. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when I gave this statement. I had several meetings with the OTP, so you may be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to ask for the clarification of a minor point which still remains after your answer to my learned friend. Is it true that you were born in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Travnik is a small town but it has a long history; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you lived in Guca Gora, a well-known place not far from Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
